svchost.exe masquerading in user Documents folder (N-able N-central compromise) AIInstallation High
Hunts for a process or dropped binary named svchost.exe living under a user's Documents directory, an explicit IOC N-able published for the N-central takeover campaign. Legitimate svchost.exe only ever executes from System32/SysWOW64, so a Documents-path copy is high-fidelity masquerading. Rationale: Uses N-able's own published IOC ('look for svchost.exe in users' Documents folders'). Legitimate svchost only launches from System32/SysWOW64, so path anchoring on Documents yields near-zero benign hits. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/n-able-says-attackers-take-over-n.html • https://www.huntress.com/blog
ATT&CKT1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Malware-analysis or reverse-engineering workstation where an analyst saved a copy of svchost.exe into a Documents folder for study
  • Backup/restore tooling that stages system binaries under a user profile during migration
  • Security-training lab machines demonstrating masquerading techniques
  • A user extracting a memory-forensics capture or triage package containing a copy of svchost.exe
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("7z.exe","winrar.exe","explorer.exe") and FolderPath has "Forensic")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the SHA256 of the Documents svchost.exe and compare to the known-good Microsoft svchost hash; check InitiatingProcessCommandLine and whether the file carries a valid Microsoft signature. 2) Contain: isolate the host, quarantine the binary, and confirm whether it is a renamed cloudflared (check for 'tunnel run'/'--token' in the command line). 3) Hunt: on the same host and other endpoints in the same N-central managed group, look for a 'Cloudflared' service, outbound port 7844, and connections to the published attacker IPs/domains.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "svchost.exe"
| where FolderPath has "Documents"
| where FolderPath !startswith "C:\\Windows"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\svchost.exe"
| where NewProcessName has "Documents"
| where NewProcessName !startswith "C:\\Windows"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Cloudflared tunnel installed as a Windows service (N-central persistence) AIInstallation High
Detects installation of a Windows service named Cloudflared or a service pointing at a cloudflared tunnel binary, the persistence mechanism N-able reported attackers registered on managed endpoints so access survived reboot and N-central revocation. Rationale: Anchored on N-able's stated IOC ('a service named Cloudflared') and the reported TTP of running Cloudflare tunnels as services for reboot persistence. Service-name/path pivot is precise and rarely benign in managed-endpoint fleets. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/n-able-says-attackers-take-over-n.html • https://www.cyber.gov.au
ATT&CKT1543.003 T1572
Data sourcesEndpoint.Services
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Organisation that legitimately uses Cloudflare Tunnel (cloudflared) for sanctioned remote access installs the service by policy
  • IT admin testing cloudflared for internal web-app publishing
  • A managed-service provider that deploys cloudflared as an approved connectivity tool
  • Automated provisioning scripts that register cloudflared on kiosk/remote hosts
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify who/what installed the service (InitiatingProcessCommandLine), the binary path/hash, and whether cloudflared is sanctioned in this environment. 2) Contain: stop and delete the service, kill the cloudflared process, and block outbound port 7844; preserve the binary and tunnel token for IR. 3) Hunt: because upgrading N-central does NOT remove this endpoint persistence, sweep every device in the same N-central account for the Cloudflared service, svchost.exe in Documents, and the published attacker IPs/domains.
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType == "ServiceInstalled"
| where AdditionalFields has "cloudflared" or AdditionalFields has "tunnel run"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, AdditionalFields, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4697
| where ServiceName has "cloudflared" or ServiceFileName has "cloudflared" or ServiceFileName has "tunnel"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ServiceName, ServiceFileName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Cloudflare tunnel outbound egress on TCP/7844 from managed endpoints AICommand & Control Medium
Detects outbound connections on TCP/7844 (Cloudflare tunnel/argotunnel control channel) or from a cloudflared process, the outbound-only C2 path attackers used so no inbound firewall rule was needed and access persisted after the N-central route was revoked. Rationale: Grounded on N-able's description of Cloudflare tunnels running as services and connecting outbound to Cloudflare's edge. TCP/7844 is cloudflared's control channel; pairing with the cloudflared process/argotunnel host raises fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/n-able-says-attackers-take-over-n.html • https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-one/connections/connect-networks/
ATT&CKT1572 T1071.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Sanctioned use of Cloudflare Tunnel for remote access or internal app publishing generates the same 7844 egress
  • Developers running 'cloudflared tunnel' for local testing
  • Cloudflare WARP client traffic on some deployments
  • MSP-approved cloudflared connectors on remote sites
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm whether cloudflared is sanctioned; identify the initiating process, service backing, and the tunnel token/hostname. 2) Contain: block TCP/7844 egress at the firewall, stop/delete the Cloudflared service, and isolate affected hosts. 3) Hunt: correlate 7844 egress with a 'Cloudflared' service, svchost.exe in Documents, and the six published attacker IPs across the N-central-managed fleet; because tunnels persist independently of N-central, remediate each endpoint.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemotePort == 7844 or InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "cloudflared.exe" or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "cloudflared" or RemoteUrl has "argotunnel.com"
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl
| order by Timestamp desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DestinationPort == 7844 or DestinationHostName has "argotunnel.com"
| project TimeGenerated, SourceHostName, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationHostName, DestinationPort, ApplicationProtocol, DeviceProduct
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Endpoint connections to N-able published attacker IPs (N-central takeover) AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts for outbound connections from managed endpoints or N-central servers to the six IP addresses N-able published for this campaign. Four are Mullvad/NordVPN exit nodes (per Huntress), so this is a hunting pivot to be correlated with N-central UI/endpoint logs, not a standalone alert. Rationale: Uses the six exact IPs N-able published. Huntress attributed four to Mullvad/NordVPN exit nodes, so this is scoped as a hunting pivot to correlate with N-central UI/network/endpoint logs rather than alert-on-first-hit. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/n-able-says-attackers-take-over-n.html • https://www.huntress.com/blog
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1090
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: high — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate employees using Mullvad or NordVPN whose exit nodes overlap four of the published IPs (per Huntress)
  • Corporate VPN concentrator sharing an ASN with a listed provider
  • Threat-intel or research boxes deliberately touching the IOCs
  • Shared cloud/VPS ranges where the IP has been reassigned since the campaign
Response runbook
1) Triage: for each hit, verify the source host is an N-central server or managed endpoint and check whether the user legitimately runs a VPN (four IPs are Mullvad/NordVPN). 2) Contain: if the host is an N-central asset or shows corroborating IOCs, isolate it and block the IP. 3) Hunt: correlate matches with ui_access_control.log / BASupSrvc logs, the Cloudflared service, and svchost.exe-in-Documents; expand to sessions tied to mspsupport@n-able.com.

| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP in ("173.249.252.200","87.249.138.34","37.19.210.32","37.153.90.88","92.118.112.181","68.235.46.214")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession

| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, NetworkApplicationProtocol, DvcAction
| order by TimeGenerated desc

DNS resolution of N-central campaign attacker DDNS domains AICommand & Control High
Detects DNS queries for the three Synology DDNS domains Huntress published for the N-central intrusion (mousears.synology.me and two direct.quickconnect.to hosts). Exact-FQDN matching makes this a high-fidelity C2/staging indicator. Rationale: Exact-FQDN match on the three attacker domains Huntress published in its August 3 rapid response. Full-domain matching (not a wildcard on synology.me/quickconnect.to) keeps FPs near zero while still catching the campaign infrastructure. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/n-able-says-attackers-take-over-n.html • https://www.huntress.com/blog
ATT&CKT1071.004 T1568
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A user who legitimately owns a Synology NAS reachable via one of these exact quickconnect.to hostnames (unlikely given the specific attacker labels)
  • Security researcher resolving the IOC for validation
  • DNS sinkhole/telemetry appliance re-querying the domains
  • Threat-intel enrichment tooling touching the FQDNs
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the querying host and the process (ContextImageFileName) that triggered the lookup; confirm it is an N-central asset or managed endpoint. 2) Contain: sinkhole/block the three FQDNs, isolate the host, and capture any cloudflared/svchost artifacts. 3) Hunt: pivot from the resolving host to the Cloudflared service, TCP/7844 egress, the published attacker IPs, and N-central Take Control logs (ui_access_control.log, BASupSrvc_*.log.gz).
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("mousears.synology.me","wagoosh.direct.quickconnect.to","who-ripped-one.direct.quickconnect.to")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
DnsEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Name has_any ("mousears.synology.me","wagoosh.direct.quickconnect.to","who-ripped-one.direct.quickconnect.to")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ClientIP, Name, QueryType, ResultCodeName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

N-able Take Control agent (BASupSrvc) spawning process enumeration on managed endpoints AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects the N-able Take Control/support agent (GetSupportService_N-Central, BASupSrvc) spawning process-enumeration tools, matching Huntress's observation that post-compromise activity was limited to enumerating running processes on reached endpoints. Flags attacker-driven remote reconnaissance through the RMM agent. Rationale: Parent binary grounded in the article's Take Control log path C:\ProgramData\GetSupportService_N-Central\Logs\BASupSrvc_*.log.gz; child behaviour grounded in Huntress's finding that post-compromise activity was limited to enumerating running processes before disconnect. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/n-able-says-attackers-take-over-n.html • https://www.huntress.com/blog
ATT&CKT1057 T1219
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate N-able Take Control session where a technician runs tasklist/Get-Process for real troubleshooting (article notes these logs appear during legitimate use)
  • Automated N-central monitoring scripts that poll running processes
  • Software-inventory or patch pre-checks executed through the RMM agent
  • Helpdesk remote support gathering process lists for a ticket
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "scheduled" and AccountName endswith "$")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull ui_access_control.log and BASupSrvc_*.log.gz for the session, and check whether it maps to an authorised technician or to an N-able support identity such as mspsupport@n-able.com. 2) Contain: if unattributed, suspend the Take Control session, rotate N-central operator credentials, and isolate the endpoint. 3) Hunt: on the same endpoint look for the Cloudflared service, svchost.exe in Documents, TCP/7844 egress, and the published IPs/domains; enumerate all nine-ish endpoints reached under the affected partner account.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("BASupSrvc.exe","BASupApp.exe","BASupSrvcUpdater.exe")
| where (FileName in~ ("tasklist.exe","wmic.exe","qprocess.exe")) or (FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe") and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("Get-Process","tasklist","process list","wmic process"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("BASupSrvc.exe","BASupApp.exe","BASupSrvcUpdater.exe")
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\tasklist.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "\\wmic.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "\\qprocess.exe" or (NewProcessName endswith "\\powershell.exe" and CommandLine has "Get-Process")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web

    [| tstats summariesonly=false count

| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time

         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",

           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",

                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.

Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"

          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Hugging Face Diffusers Flaws Could Let Model Repositories Execute Arbitrary Code

The Hacker News
2026-08-03 11 use cases 4 techniques 4 kill-chain phases detected

Three high-severity security flaws have been disclosed in Hugging Face's Diffusers library that could allow crafted model repositories to stealthily execute arbitrary code on machines that load it, opening the artificial intelligence (AI) supply chain to security risk. "These vulnerabilities are bypassing trust_remote_code, the safeguard designed to stop unreviewed code from running in the

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Untrusted custom-pipeline .py (incl. None.py) staged in Hugging Face cache — FaceHugger · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Python/Diffusers process spawning shell or download utility (FaceHugger RCE execution) · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Hugging Face Diffusers Flaws Could Let Model Repositories Execute Arbitrary Code
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Outbound C2/exfil from Python after Diffusers model load (non-Hugging-Face egress) · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Untrusted custom-pipeline .py (incl. None.py) staged in Hugging Face cache — FaceHugger AIDelivery High
Hunts the FaceHugger (CVE-2026-44827/44513/45804) trust_remote_code bypass, where DiffusionPipeline.from_pretrained pulls a crafted repo that drops executable Python (notably a pipeline literally named None.py, or stray *.py under model component subdirs like unet/ and scheduler/) into the local Hugging Face snapshot/dynamic-module cache. A model snapshot should be weights + JSON — a .py file appearing under it, written by a python interpreter, is the pre-execution artifact of the bypass. Rationale: Uses the article's exact bypass artifacts: the crafted custom_pipeline named None.py (CVE-2026-44827) and the maintainer guidance to inspect snapshots for unexpected *.py under unet/, scheduler/, etc. A .py written by python into the HF cache is high-fidelity because legitimate model snapshots ship weights + JSON, not code.
ATT&CKT1195.001 T1059.006
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate custom pipelines from trusted, audited repos that intentionally ship pipeline.py (e.g. community diffusion pipelines the team explicitly uses)
  • Diffusers itself caching its own dynamic modules for a first-party trusted pipeline
  • Data scientist manually copying a reviewed pipeline.py into the local snapshot for testing
  • A repo with a benign helper .py placed at the snapshot root that the team has vetted
Suppression filter
| where not (FolderPath has_any ("stabilityai","runwayml","CompVis") and InitiatingProcessAccountName in~ ("approved-mlops","ci-builder"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: open the written .py (None.py or the component-subdir file) and read it — look for os.system/subprocess/exec/eval, urllib/requests, base64 blobs. Identify the model repo id from the parent folder path and the InitiatingProcessCommandLine. 2) Contain: isolate the host if the file contains execution/network code; kill the python process; quarantine the file and the whole model snapshot dir; block the source repo. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same host/user for child shells spawned by python (UC2) and outbound connections from python (UC3) within minutes of the write; check whether Diffusers < 0.38.0 is installed across the fleet.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where FileName endswith ".py"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\.cache\huggingface\", "/.cache/huggingface/", "diffusers_modules", @"\huggingface\hub\", "/huggingface/hub/")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("python.exe","pythonw.exe","python","python3")
| where FileName =~ "None.py" or FolderPath has_any ("unet","scheduler","vae","text_encoder","tokenizer","feature_extractor","safety_checker")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where TargetFileName endswith ".py"
| where TargetFilePath has_any ("huggingface", "diffusers_modules")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("python","python3","pythonw")
| where TargetFileName =~ "None.py" or TargetFilePath has_any ("unet","scheduler","vae","text_encoder","tokenizer","feature_extractor","safety_checker")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFileSHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Untrusted Python custom-pipeline file staged in Hugging Face cache (FaceHugger)
id: 8f3c9e21-4a6d-4c7b-9b2e-1d5f6a7c8e90

references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/hugging-face-diffusers-flaws-could-let.html

date: 2026/08/03
tags:

  - attack.t1059.006

  category: file_event
  product: windows

  selection_path:
    TargetFilename|contains:
      - '\.cache\huggingface\'
      - 'diffusers_modules'
      - '\huggingface\hub\'
  selection_ext:
    TargetFilename|endswith: '.py'
  selection_proc:

      - '\python.exe'
      - '\pythonw.exe'

#event_simpleName=FileWritten

Python/Diffusers process spawning shell or download utility (FaceHugger RCE execution) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts the arbitrary-code-execution stage of FaceHugger: once trust_remote_code is bypassed, the crafted custom pipeline runs inside the loading python process and typically spawns a shell or grabs a second stage. Flags a python parent spawning bash/sh/cmd/powershell where the child command line carries download or encoding indicators — the point where a routine DiffusionPipeline.from_pretrained turns into an initial-access vector. Rationale: Directly targets the article's core claim — crafted model repos 'stealthily execute arbitrary code on machines that load it'. Python (the Diffusers host) spawning a shell/downloader with second-stage indicators is the observable RCE moment; the encoding/network indicators keep FPs down versus a bare python->shell rule.
ATT&CKT1059.004 T1059.001 T1059.006
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • ML build/setup scripts where python legitimately shells out to curl/wget to fetch datasets or wheels
  • Jupyter/IPython '!' bang commands that spawn a shell with curl/wget
  • conda/pip post-install hooks invoking bash with base64-encoded config
  • CI pipeline python wrappers that call powershell -enc for legitimate packaging
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("jupyter","ipykernel_launcher","conda","pip install","setup.py","pip._internal") )
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the parent python command line and the child command line; decode any base64/-enc payload; determine whether python was loading a Diffusers pipeline (check recent HF cache writes on the host, UC1). 2) Contain: isolate the host and kill both processes if the decoded command reaches an external IP or drops a binary; preserve the parent python script and any staged .py. 3) Hunt: enumerate outbound connections from the same python PID/host (UC3), check other hosts that pulled the same model repo id, and confirm Diffusers version — upgrade to >=0.38.0.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("python.exe","pythonw.exe","python","python3")
| where FileName in~ ("bash","sh","dash","zsh","cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","curl","wget","nc","ncat")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("curl","wget","/dev/tcp","base64","-enc","Invoke-WebRequest","IEX","ncat","nc ","bash -i","socket.socket","python -c")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("python.exe","pythonw.exe","python","python3")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("bash","sh","dash","zsh","cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","curl","wget","ncat")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("curl","wget","/dev/tcp","base64","-enc","Invoke-WebRequest","IEX","ncat","nc ","bash -i","socket.socket","python -c")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Outbound C2/exfil from Python after Diffusers model load (non-Hugging-Face egress) AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts post-exploitation network activity from the python process that loaded a malicious Diffusers pipeline (FaceHugger). Surfaces DNS/HTTP egress from python to destinations that are NOT Hugging Face / PyPI / model-CDN infrastructure — beaconing or second-stage retrieval driven by attacker code that ran during from_pretrained. Pairs with UC1 (file staging) and UC2 (subprocess) as the C2 leg of the chain. Rationale: The article states a bypassed model load 'can easily become a vector for arbitrary code execution' running in the user's process; python egress to anything other than the known model/package CDNs is the natural C2/exfil observable. Excluding HF/PyPI/pytorch CDNs isolates the anomalous destinations.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1041
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Python apps legitimately calling third-party APIs (OpenAI, internal REST services, telemetry endpoints)
  • MLflow / Weights & Biases / HuggingFace-datasets pulling from non-CDN mirrors
  • pip resolving a wheel from a private/internal index not in the allowlist
  • Data pipelines fetching training data from S3/GCS buckets
Suppression filter
| where not (RemoteUrl has_any ("openai.com","wandb.ai","mlflow","s3.amazonaws.com","storage.googleapis.com") )
Response runbook
1) Triage: check whether the destination is newly-registered/rare-in-org and whether the same host shows a recent HF cache .py write (UC1) or python->shell spawn (UC2) minutes prior. 2) Contain: block the destination domain/IP at egress, isolate the host if correlated with UC1/UC2, and snapshot the python process memory/args. 3) Hunt: sweep the fleet for other python hosts contacting the same destination and for the originating model repo id; confirm and patch Diffusers to >=0.38.0.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("python.exe","pythonw.exe","python","python3")
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| where isnotempty(RemoteUrl)
| where not(RemoteUrl has_any ("huggingface.co","hf.co","pythonhosted.org","pypi.org","cloudfront.net","githubusercontent.com","pytorch.org","anaconda.com"))
| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), Count=count(), Ports=make_set(RemotePort,10) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by FirstSeen desc
// Microsoft Sentinel — auto-derived from the Defender XDR hunt.
// Requires the Microsoft 365 Defender data connector (streams the
// advanced-hunting tables into Sentinel; Timestamp → TimeGenerated).
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("python.exe","pythonw.exe","python","python3")
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| where isnotempty(RemoteUrl)
| where not(RemoteUrl has_any ("huggingface.co","hf.co","pythonhosted.org","pypi.org","cloudfront.net","githubusercontent.com","pytorch.org","anaconda.com"))
| summarize FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), Count=count(), Ports=make_set(RemotePort,10) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by FirstSeen desc
title: Python process DNS query to non-Hugging-Face destination (FaceHugger C2)
id: c93f18d7-2e40-4b6a-8f11-7a2d5c9e4b03
description: Detects DNS resolutions initiated by a python interpreter to destinations outside known Hugging Face / PyPI / model-CDN infrastructure, indicating C2 or second-stage retrieval after a malicious Diffusers pipeline executed (FaceHugger).
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/hugging-face-diffusers-flaws-could-let.html
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/08/03
tags:

  - attack.t1041
logsource:
  category: dns
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\python.exe'
      - '\pythonw.exe'
  filter_known:
    QueryName|contains:
      - 'huggingface.co'
      - 'hf.co'
      - 'pythonhosted.org'
      - 'pypi.org'
      - 'cloudfront.net'
  condition: selection and not filter_known
level: medium
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:3 (@Image:(*\python.exe OR *\Python.exe OR *\pythonw.exe)) -(@DestinationHostname:(*huggingface.co OR *hf.co OR *pythonhosted.org OR *pypi.org OR *cloudfront.net OR *githubusercontent.com))
#event_simpleName=DnsRequest
| ContextImageFileName=/python(3|w)?(\.exe)?$/i
| NOT (DomainName=/(huggingface\.co|hf\.co|pythonhosted\.org|pypi\.org|cloudfront\.net|githubusercontent\.com|pytorch\.org)$/i)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, DomainName, ContextImageFileName], function=count())
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where (All_Traffic.app IN ("python.exe","pythonw.exe","python","python3") OR All_Traffic.process_name IN ("python.exe","pythonw.exe","python","python3")) All_Traffic.direction="outbound" by All_Traffic.dest All_Traffic.dest_ip All_Traffic.dest_port All_Traffic.src All_Traffic.process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)` | search NOT (dest="*huggingface.co" OR dest="*hf.co" OR dest="*pythonhosted.org" OR dest="*pypi.org" OR dest="*cloudfront.net") | `ctime(firstTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where (All_Traffic.app IN ("python.exe","pythonw.exe","python","python3") OR All_Traffic.process_name IN ("python.exe","pythonw.exe","python","python3")) All_Traffic.direction="outbound" by All_Traffic.dest All_Traffic.dest_ip All_Traffic.dest_port All_Traffic.src All_Traffic.process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)` | search NOT (dest="*huggingface.co" OR dest="*hf.co" OR dest="*pythonhosted.org" OR dest="*pypi.org" OR dest="*cloudfront.net") | `ctime(firstTime)`

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web

| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`

    [| tstats summariesonly=false count

    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time

         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

status: experimental
description: |

    user to press Win+R and paste a payload. The result is
    powershell/mshta launched directly from explorer.exe with iex /
    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:

    category: process_creation

Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Active Storage crafted image upload to libvips variant endpoints (CVE-2026-66066) · [LLM] Exposure hunt: hosts with vulnerable libvips / Rails Active Storage (CVE-2026-66066)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Rails app worker spawning shell or network child (KindaRails2Shell RCE)
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Rails/Ruby worker reading secret_key_base and credential files post-upload (CVE-2026-66066) · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs
Active Storage crafted image upload to libvips variant endpoints (CVE-2026-66066) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts unauthenticated traffic to Rails Active Storage upload and variant/representation endpoints, the exploitation surface for CVE-2026-66066 (KindaRails2Shell) where a crafted image drives libvips into an arbitrary-file-read. Surfaces sources that both submit uploads and request server-side image processing so an analyst can triage the file-read primitive. Rationale: Uses the canonical Rails Active Storage route prefixes (/rails/active_storage/direct_uploads, /representations/, /blobs/, /disk/) — corroborated by Rapid7/Ethiack as the direct-upload + variant-processing surface. Technical PoC strings were withheld by the researchers, so this is a triage hunt on the exploit surface rather than a signature. Cross-checked against: • https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/etr-kindarails2shell-cve-2026-66066-critical-arbitrary-file-read-and-possible-remote-code-execution-in-ruby-on-rails/ • https://ethiack.com/info-hub/research/kindarails2shell-rails-rce-cve-2026-66066 • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/critical-rails-flaw-could-let.html
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate users uploading avatars/profile pictures and viewing generated thumbnails
  • Load/synthetic monitoring hitting upload endpoints
  • CDN or image-proxy warming Active Storage representations in bulk
  • Mobile app clients using direct_uploads at high volume
  • Security scanners (internal ASM/DAST) probing the same routes
Suppression filter
| where isnotempty(SrcIpAddr) and SrcIpAddr !in ("127.0.0.1", "::1")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the raw requests for the top source IPs — check whether they are unauthenticated, whether upload requests are immediately followed by representation/variant requests, and whether responses are anomalously sized (leaked file content). 2) Contain: if libvips <8.13 or the app is unpatched (Rails <7.2.3.2/8.0.5.1/8.1.3.1), block the source at the WAF/reverse-proxy and enable VIPS_BLOCK_UNTRUSTED. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same host to UC 'Rails worker sensitive-file access' and 'Rails worker spawning shell/network child' to confirm file-read and RCE.
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Url has "/rails/active_storage/"
| where Url has_any ("/representations/", "/blobs/", "/direct_uploads", "/disk/")
| summarize Requests = count(), Methods = make_set(HttpMethod, 10), Statuses = make_set(HttpStatusCode, 10), SampleUrls = make_set(Url, 10), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by SrcIpAddr, HttpHostName
| order by LastSeen desc

Rails/Ruby worker reading secret_key_base and credential files post-upload (CVE-2026-66066) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects the Rails application process (ruby/puma/unicorn/passenger) accessing sensitive secret and environment files — the credential-access step of CVE-2026-66066 where the libvips arbitrary-file-read is used to exfiltrate secret_key_base, master.key, credentials.yml.enc, .env and /proc/self/environ. High-fidelity because a running web worker should not be reading these at request time. Rationale: Ties the standard Rails secret paths named in the article (secret_key_base, master.key, database/cloud creds in the process environment) to the app-server process identity — a Rails worker reading /proc/self/environ or master.key at runtime is the direct fingerprint of the file-read primitive being abused. Cross-checked against: • https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/etr-kindarails2shell-cve-2026-66066-critical-arbitrary-file-read-and-possible-remote-code-execution-in-ruby-on-rails/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/critical-rails-flaw-could-let.html • https://socprime.com/blog/cve-2026-66066-critical-rails-flaw-exposes-server-files-via-image-uploads/
ATT&CKT1552.001 T1552
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Normal app boot reading config/master.key and credentials.yml.enc during initialization (baseline once per deploy/restart)
  • dotenv gems loading .env at startup
  • Config-management/CI tooling templating credential files
  • APM/observability agents enumerating process environment
  • Developer console (rails c) sessions on a jump host
Suppression filter
| where ActionType != "FileCreated" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "rails console" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "assets:precompile"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the access is at request-serving time (not process boot) and correlate the host/timestamp with UC1 Active Storage upload traffic within the same window. 2) Contain: treat secret_key_base, DB and Active Storage credentials as compromised — rotate them, rotate the Rails master key, and patch to Rails 7.2.3.2/8.0.5.1/8.1.3.1 with libvips ≥8.13. 3) Hunt: search for forged session cookies / anomalous authenticated sessions and pivot to UC3 for shell/network children of the worker.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("ruby", "puma", "unicorn", "passenger", "bundle", "rails")
| where FileName in~ ("credentials.yml.enc", "master.key", "environ", ".env")
    or FolderPath has_any ("/config/credentials", "/proc/self/environ")
| where FolderPath !startswith "/tmp/" and FolderPath !has "/active_storage/"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessId, FileName, FolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("ruby", "puma", "unicorn", "passenger", "bundle", "rails")
| where TargetFilePath has_any ("/config/credentials.yml.enc", "/config/master.key", "/config/credentials/", "/proc/self/environ")
    or TargetFileName =~ ".env"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessId, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Rails app worker spawning shell or network child (KindaRails2Shell RCE) AIInstallation High
Detects the Rails/Ruby application server (puma/unicorn/passenger/ruby) spawning an unexpected shell or network client (sh, bash, curl, wget, nc, python, ruby -e) — the RCE execution stage where a forged, secret_key_base-signed serialized payload drives insecure deserialization into command execution on the host. Rationale: A web application worker (puma/unicorn/passenger/ruby) is not expected to fork shells or curl/wget at runtime; pairing that specific parent set with shell/network children is the highest-fidelity signal of the deserialization-to-RCE endgame the article and Akamai describe. Cross-checked against: • https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/etr-kindarails2shell-cve-2026-66066-critical-arbitrary-file-read-and-possible-remote-code-execution-in-ruby-on-rails/ • https://ethiack.com/info-hub/research/kindarails2shell-rails-rce-cve-2026-66066
ATT&CKT1059.004 T1059
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Rails app legitimately shelling out to ImageMagick/ffmpeg/git via system() for background jobs
  • Sidekiq/Resque workers running rake tasks that invoke curl/bash
  • Health-check or entrypoint scripts (bash) launched by the app container
  • Deploy hooks calling shell from within the app process
  • Ruby scripts using backticks for legitimate ops tooling
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("convert", "identify", "vipsthumbnail", "ffmpeg", "/rake", "sidekiq", "healthcheck"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the child command line — reverse-shell one-liners, curl to unknown IPs, or writes to /tmp are strong TP indicators; benign image/rake tooling is FP. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the spawned process tree, and treat app secrets as compromised (rotate secret_key_base + all DB/cloud creds). 3) Hunt: pull outbound connections from the child, correlate back to the originating Active Storage upload (UC1) and credential-file reads (UC2), and search other Rails hosts for the same parent→child pattern.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("ruby", "puma", "unicorn", "passenger", "rails", "bundle")
| where FileName in~ ("sh", "bash", "dash", "curl", "wget", "nc", "ncat", "python", "python3", "perl")
    or (FileName in~ ("ruby") and ProcessCommandLine has "-e ")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("ruby", "puma", "unicorn", "passenger", "rails", "bundle")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("/sh", "/bash", "/dash", "/curl", "/wget", "/nc", "/ncat", "/python", "/perl")
    or (ActingProcessName has "/ruby" and ActingProcessCommandLine has "-e ")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Exposure hunt: hosts with vulnerable libvips / Rails Active Storage (CVE-2026-66066) AIExploitation High
Surfaces internet-facing hosts still exposed to CVE-2026-66066 — libvips before 8.13 (which cannot disable the unfuzzed operations at all) or unpatched Rails Active Storage. Drives pre-exploitation prioritization since public PoCs are already circulating. Rationale: Directly keys on the article's named CVE (CVE-2026-66066) and the libvips 8.13 fix floor; scoping to internet-facing hosts turns the vuln feed into an actionable, prioritized exposure list ahead of the disclosed public PoCs. Cross-checked against: • https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/etr-kindarails2shell-cve-2026-66066-critical-arbitrary-file-read-and-possible-remote-code-execution-in-ruby-on-rails/ • https://www.linuxcompatible.org/story/rails-7232-8051-and-8131-active-storage-security-patch-targets-cve202666066
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities.Vulnerabilities
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Hosts that use ImageMagick (not libvips) as the Active Storage processor — not actually exploitable
  • Apps that do not accept untrusted image uploads (internal-only) — lower real risk
  • TVM version-string mismatch flagging a backported/distro-patched libvips as vulnerable
  • Rails 6.x using Active Storage defaults (not affected) still flagged by generic version match
  • Decommissioned/quarantined hosts still in inventory
Response runbook
1) Triage: for each flagged host confirm it uses the vips processor and accepts untrusted uploads (else de-prioritize), and check internet exposure. 2) Contain: patch Active Storage to 7.2.3.2/8.0.5.1/8.1.3.1, upgrade libvips to ≥8.13, and set VIPS_BLOCK_UNTRUSTED / Vips.block_untrusted(true); apply WAF virtual patch where immediate upgrade isn't possible. 3) Hunt: retro-scan UC1/UC2/UC3 telemetry on every exposed host for prior exploitation before the patch window.

| join kind=leftouter (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d) | summarize arg_max(Timestamp, IsInternetFacing, OSPlatform) by DeviceId) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, IsInternetFacing, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by IsInternetFacing desc, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc

Adform crypto-swap stealer C2/exfil beacon to 84.32.102.230:7744 AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts endpoint or perimeter connections to the hardcoded attacker server 84.32.102.230 on TCP/7744, the exfil endpoint the poisoned Adform trackpoint-async.js beacons to on page load (sending victim hostname + path). This IP:port is the single highest-fidelity IOC of the campaign — it exists only in the malicious payload. Rationale: 84.32.102.230:7744 is the exact exfil IP:port confirmed across the article and second sources (BleepingComputer, Beaumont/DoublePulsar). A raw-IP non-standard-port destination with no legitimate business use makes this near-zero-FP.   • Security researcher / malware sandbox detonating the captured sample from a corporate range
  • Threat-intel scanners or blue-team validation traffic deliberately hitting the IOC
  • IP reallocated to a benign host after the campaign is taken down (validate against WHOIS/first-seen date)
  • Internal proxy or NAT gateway appearing as the source, collapsing many users behind one src_ip
Suppression filter
| where not (DeviceName in~ ("sandbox-detonation-01","malware-lab-01"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the source host/user and confirm the initiating process is a browser (msedge/chrome/firefox); pull the RemoteUrl/referrer the browser was on to find which affected website served the poisoned script. 2) Contain: block 84.32.102.230 at egress/firewall, and instruct the user to clear browser cache (the malicious trackpoint-async.js may persist cached) and verify any crypto wallet addresses recently copied/pasted. 3) Hunt: pivot to all hosts that both loaded s2.adform.net/banners/scripts/st/trackpoint-async.js and beaconed to this IP; alert any user who transacted crypto on July 26-27 2026.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where RemoteIP == "84.32.102.230"
| where RemotePort == 7744
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, LocalIP
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where DstIpAddr == "84.32.102.230"
| where DstPortNumber == 7744
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, SrcUsername, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, NetworkApplicationProtocol, Url, DvcAction, DvcHostname
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Adform Crypto-Swap Stealer C2 Beacon to 84.32.102.230:7744

description: Detects outbound connection to the hardcoded exfil server used by the poisoned Adform trackpoint-async.js crypto-wallet swapper.

Confirmed Adform supply-chain victim: poisoned script load + beacon to attacker IP AIDelivery High
Correlates hosts that loaded the compromised third-party resource s2.adform.net/banners/scripts/st/trackpoint-async.js with an outbound beacon to 84.32.102.230 on the same host. The script load alone is benign (Adform is loaded by thousands of legitimate sites); the join with the exfil beacon promotes it to a confirmed supply-chain compromise. Rationale: Combines the two confirmed IOCs (poisoned file path s2.adform.net/.../trackpoint-async.js and exfil IP 84.32.102.230:7744) on a single host. The join eliminates the massive benign-load noise of Adform being a legitimate ad tag, yielding a high-fidelity supply-chain-victim signal. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/online-ad-firm-adforms-script-compromised-to-steal-cryptocurrency/ • https://doublepulsar.com/adform-compromised-to-serve-crypto-stealer-via-supply-chain-attack-2f1ec024f33e
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1189
Data sourcesWeb.Web Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Shared egress/NAT IP causes an unrelated user's script load to correlate with another user's beacon (validate on managed-host DeviceId join in Defender rather than SrcIpAddr)
  • Proxy that rewrites/caches the Adform URL so the recorded host differs from the beaconing host
  • IOC IP reallocated post-takedown to a benign service
  • Falcon variant relies on DNS to s2.adform.net which is a shared CDN host — treat DNS as a weak loader proxy, the beacon is the anchor
Response runbook
1) Triage: for each correlated host confirm the beacon process is a browser and identify the affected first-party website that embedded the tag. 2) Contain: block 84.32.102.230 at egress, force browser cache clear on the host, and reset/verify any crypto wallet addresses the user handled. 3) Hunt: enumerate every user who initiated crypto transactions during the exposure window and review outbound transfers for address substitution; notify affected clients per IR policy.

    | where Timestamp > ago(14d)
    | where RemoteUrl has "trackpoint-async.js" and RemoteUrl has "adform"
    | distinct DeviceId, DeviceName;
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where RemoteIP == "84.32.102.230" and RemotePort == 7744
| join kind=inner ScriptLoaders on DeviceId
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
let ScriptLoaders = ImWebSession
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
    | where Url has "trackpoint-async.js" and HttpHostName has "adform"
    | distinct SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname;
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where DstIpAddr == "84.32.102.230" and DstPortNumber == 7744
| join kind=inner ScriptLoaders on SrcIpAddr
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, NetworkApplicationProtocol
| order by TimeGenerated desc
#event_simpleName=DnsRequest DomainName=/s2\.adform\.net/i
| join({#event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP4 RemoteAddressIP4="84.32.102.230" RemotePort=7744}, field=aid, include=[RemoteAddressIP4])
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName], function=count())
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count from datamodel=Web.Web where Web.url="*trackpoint-async.js*" AND Web.site="*adform*" by Web.src Web.url | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | join type=inner src [ | tstats summariesonly=true count as beaconCount from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where All_Traffic.dest_ip="84.32.102.230" AND All_Traffic.dest_port=7744 by All_Traffic.src | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)` | rename src as src ] | table src url count beaconCount
| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Web.Web where Web.url="*trackpoint-async.js*" AND Web.site="*adform*" by Web.src Web.url | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | join type=inner src [ | tstats summariesonly=false count as beaconCount from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where All_Traffic.dest_ip="84.32.102.230" AND All_Traffic.dest_port=7744 by All_Traffic.src | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)` | rename src as src ] | table src url count beaconCount
Exposure scoping: hosts that loaded poisoned Adform trackpoint-async.js (Jul 26-28 2026) AIDelivery Medium
IR-scoping hunt that surfaces every managed host which fetched s2.adform.net/banners/scripts/st/trackpoint-async.js during the compromise window (oldest malicious sample July 26, removed July 27 2026). Used to build the affected-user list for cache-clear guidance and crypto-transaction review, not as a standalone malicious-behaviour alert. Rationale: Anchored on the exact compromised resource path (s2.adform.net/.../trackpoint-async.js) and the confirmed malicious window (sample July 26, removed July 27 2026). Deliberately scoped by date because the file was benign before/after — this is an exposure list, not a malicious-behaviour detection, hence hunting tier and high expected FP. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/online-ad-firm-adforms-script-compromised-to-steal-cryptocurrency/ • https://doublepulsar.com/adform-compromised-to-serve-crypto-stealer-via-supply-chain-attack-2f1ec024f33e
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1189
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: high — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Hosts that loaded the clean, restored trackpoint-async.js after Adform's July 27 fix (mitigated by the date window)
  • Legitimate marketing/ad-ops staff and QA whose job involves the Adform platform
  • Cached copies replayed after the window, skewing timestamps
  • FDR/Falcon variant keys on DNS to shared host s2.adform.net which serves many benign scripts — treat as broad exposure, not confirmation
Suppression filter
| where FirstSeen between (datetime(2026-07-26) .. datetime(2026-07-28))
Response runbook
1) Triage: treat the output as the exposed-population list; prioritise hosts/users known to handle cryptocurrency. 2) Contain: push guidance to clear browser cache (the poisoned file may remain cached) and to re-verify any wallet address before sending funds. 3) Hunt: cross-reference this list against UC 'Confirmed Adform supply-chain victim' (beacon to 84.32.102.230) to separate merely-exposed from confirmed-compromised, and review crypto transactions initiated during the window for address substitution.
DeviceNetworkEvents

| where RemoteUrl has "trackpoint-async.js" and RemoteUrl has "adform"
| summarize FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp), Hits = count() by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, RemoteUrl
| order by LastSeen desc
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated between (datetime(2026-07-26) .. datetime(2026-07-28))
| where Url has "trackpoint-async.js" and HttpHostName has "adform"
| summarize FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated), Hits = count() by SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, SrcUsername
| order by LastSeen desc
